title: How do planes fly?
subtitle: Flight physics
subject: sciences
description: A plane weighing several hundred tons flies. It's not magic: it's a matter of wing shape, speed and forces balancing each other.

hero.hook: Heavier than a truck, and yet it stays in the air. Here's how.

blocks.text: A large airliner can weigh **hundreds of tones**. How can something so heavy stay in the air? The answer lies in the shape of the wings and the speed of the plane.
Four main forces are at play: **thrust** (forward), **drag** (air braking), **weight** (downward), and **lift** (upward).
Seen from the side, an airplane wing is not flat. The top is more rounded than the bottom. When the plane is moving fast, the air must go around this shape.

blocks.caption: The profile of the wing creates the lift that lifts the plane.

blocks.text: The air passing above accelerates a little. His pressure drops. Under the wing, the pressure remains stronger. This difference pushes the wing upwards: this is the **lift**. It is often explained with the principle of **Bernoulli**, named after an 18th century scholar, and with the fact that the wing also deflects the air downward.
Without speed, not enough air passing over the wing, not enough lift. This is why a plane needs a long runway to take off: the engines must accelerate it hard enough.
Birds use the same general idea: their wings create lift. But they flap their wings to move forward. The plane moves forward thanks to its engines.
In cruise flight, lift balances weight. The thrust of the engines balances the air drag. The plane then moves forward at an approximately constant speed.

To climb, the pilot (or on-board computer) tilts the nose up a little and adjusts the thrust. To descend, we often reduce the thrust. To turn, the plane is tilted to the side using movable parts of the wings, the ailerons.
When landing, we slow down. Flaps extend from the wing to increase lift at low speeds. Then the wheels touch the ground, and the brakes (sometimes also thrust reversers) stop the plane.
A helium balloon floats because it is less dense than air. A plane, no: it is much denser. It flies because it **strength** looks like it carries it, thanks to its speed and the shape of its wings.
An airplane flies thanks to the **lift** created by its wings moving through the air. Speed ​​is essential: without it, the wing no longer “pushes” enough upwards to compensate for the weight.
